question: The URDF declares tyre contact stiffness and friction through a Gazebo-classic <gazebo reference> block. Does gz-sim with DART honour them?
answer: Friction is honoured. Contact stiffness and damping are silently ignored.

conversion.converted_by: gz sdf -p over the expanded URDF
conversion.note: the parameters land under <ode>, and the world selects no engine, so gz-sim loads its default DART plugin

binary_inspection.reading: the plugin looks up slip1/slip2/fdir1/restitution_coefficient by element name and never looks up kp/kd. Absence of mu/mu2 strings proves nothing, because friction is reached through sdformat's typed accessors, which is why the empirical tests below were run.

experiment_contact_stiffness.setup: 100 kg sphere of radius 0.5 m resting on a static plane, DART, 1 ms step, 40 s simulated
experiment_contact_stiffness.conclusion: kp and kd have no effect. Tyre contact is a rigid DART constraint with no compliance.

experiment_friction.setup: 10 kg 0.4 m cube on a 20 degree ramp (tan = 0.364), same mu on both bodies, 5 s simulated
experiment_friction.conclusion: mu and mu2 are honoured: the low-friction case slid 33.5 m, the high-friction case did not move

consequences: The vehicle has no tyre compliance at all. Every bit of compliance comes from the suspension springs (8000 N/m per wheel). A reader of the URDF would reasonably assume 1e6 N/m of tyre stiffness that has never existed.

A rigid cylinder on a rigid triangle mesh is the configuration in which an internal-edge contact artefact produces an unbounded one-step impulse, because nothing absorbs it. This is plausibly the enabling condition for the single-step scan-motion rejection recorded in scan_motion_single_step.json, though that link is not proven.

The suspension damping comparison (750/1000/1200 N.s/m) and the pitch and roll measurements were all taken on a model with no tyre compliance. Those measurements stand as taken; what they do not include is the filtering a real tyre would apply to edge impulses of this kind.
not_addressed: No change has been made. Whether to model tyre compliance, and how, is a separate decision; DART exposes contact surface parameters through gz-physics, and the SDF elements it does honour are slip1, slip2, fdir1 and restitution_coefficient.
